description: Sometimes, what dogs offer people is much greater than what people can offer them. Rows of yoga mats are laid out neatly, but soon a dozen puppies bring some mischief to the scene as they run over the mats and crawl under yogis' legs. Most participants have stopped following the instructor. Some pause to pet the dogs, while others offer their laps to the curious visitors. Everyone is smiling. "I'm used to doing yoga on my own," the instructor joked midway through the class. For around 70 minutes
title: Paws on the yoga mat

description: Good butter comes from good milk — a principle that has shaped French baking traditions for centuries and is now finding new ground in Korean cuisine. Butter has become a staple of Korea's growing dessert scene, with locally adapted creations such as salt bread and butter tteok drawing long lines of customers, including international visitors. As interest in butter grows, more consumers are paying attention to its quality and seeking other ingredients to pair it with to improve their gastronomic
title: Butter is having a moment in Korea

description: A buffet bill for a family of four could approach 1 million won this Christmas, as major hotels raise their prices ahead of the year-end holiday season. Buffet prices are climbing by as much as 13.6 percent from the same period last year, with luxury hotels citing rising operating costs and demand for premium dining experiences. title: Seoul hotel buffets hike year-end prices

description: Forget the KTX. The high-speed train is a fast way to get around the country, but there are other, more scenic rail options that let passengers fully take in their surroundings. The beauty of these sightseeing trains comes from their slowness. While the KTX takes you across the country at break-neck speed, the V-train winds through the mountains at speeds as low as 20 kilometers per hour. title: Take the slow train

description: Korean retailers no longer treat Seoul as the only game in town. More are fanning out to regional cities, especially Busan, where a tourism surge opens new ground for growth. By late October, Korea had already topped last year’s record count of foreign visitors, and many now land outside Seoul to begin with.
